title: Bio & Health | September 29, 2026
summary: A thin edition: two research developments cleared the evidence bar today; routine health and lifestyle headlines were left out.

stories.headline: A Zoonotic Orthonairovirus from Febrile Patients in China
stories.dek: A newly described tick-borne virus was identified in a study of febrile patients in China.
tldr: The New England Journal of Medicine paper describes a zoonotic orthonairovirus identified in febrile patients in China.
The study reports that 10.4% of 3,163 sampled patients tested positive for the virus, based on viral RNA or IgM antibodies.
The paper and its coverage describe coinfections with Dabie bandavirus as associated with more severe complications.

body.text: The study identified Asian longhorned tick nairovirus in patients with febrile illness, using sequencing and viral isolation. The authors describe it as a distinct orthonairovirus.

Among 3,163 patients in the reported study, 10.4% tested positive for the virus; the paper also reports its detection in sampled ticks across multiple Chinese provinces. These findings characterize the study population and do not establish prevalence outside it.

The coverage notes that coinfected patients had more complications than patients with Dabie bandavirus alone. The authors say the viruses share regions and a tick vector, raising a diagnostic distinction for affected areas.

stories.whyItMatters: Identifying a second tick-borne virus in a region where another febrile disease circulates adds a pathogen-surveillance and diagnostic question.
stories.editorNote: The headline follows the peer-reviewed paper. Epidemiologic estimates are limited to the sampled patients and ticks.

stories.headline: Durability of CRISPR-Cas9 Gene Editing Targeting ANGPTL3 with CTX310
stories.dek: A 15-participant phase 1a study reported sustained lipid reductions one year after a single infusion.
tldr: The phase 1a study evaluated a one-time CTX310 infusion in people with lipid disorders.
At the highest dose, the study reported 52.5% lower LDL cholesterol and 47.8% lower triglycerides from baseline at 12 months.
The small early-stage trial reports biomarker changes and one year of follow-up; it does not establish long-term clinical outcomes.

body.text: The New England Journal of Medicine report describes a phase 1a trial of CRISPR-Cas9 editing targeting ANGPTL3. Cleveland Clinic says the trial included 15 patients and assessed whether earlier lipid reductions persisted through 12 months.
At the highest dose, the report gives reductions from baseline of 52.5% for LDL cholesterol and 47.8% for triglycerides after one year. The study was supported by CRISPR Therapeutics.
This is early-stage evidence from a small study with one year of follow-up. The sources do not report whether the observed lipid changes reduce cardiovascular events over longer periods.

stories.whyItMatters: The result is a clinical-stage test of durable in-vivo gene editing, with implications for biotech development while long-term outcomes remain unknown.
stories.editorNote: No medical recommendation is implied; report results as trial findings and preserve the phase 1a and sample-size context.
